reconcile.note: Gill harmonizes the accounts by positing three separate blind men healed across two encounters near Jericho, matching each gospel's count and location.

discrepancy.note: Strauss presses both the count and the locality: Matthew has two blind men, the others one, and Luke sets the cure entering Jericho while Matthew and Mark set it leaving.

quotes.text: Matthew having two blind men, the two other Evangelists only one; and also as to its locality, Luke making it take place on the entrance of Jesus into Jericho, Matthew and Mark on his departure out of Jericho.
quotes.attr: David Friedrich Strauss (d. 1874), The Life of Jesus Critically Examined, trans. George Eliot (1846), ch. on the cure of the blind man at Jericho, on Mark 10:46 and Luke 18:35.

sides.snippet: As he went out from Jericho, with his disciples and a great multitude
sides.verseText: They came to Jericho. As he went out from Jericho, with his disciples and a great multitude, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road.

sides.snippet: as he came near Jericho, a certain blind man sat by the road, begging.
sides.verseText: It happened, as he came near Jericho, a certain blind man sat by the road, begging.
